The turnbased rogue-like autobattler/deckbuilder idea is great, but undermined by poor autobattler AI. I've lost many runs to my troops killing picking a path onto a tile that causes them to kill themselves rather than picking a tile that would lead to winning. There's a feature which lets you see your in-game troops' movements ahead of time, but there is no way to see "if I place this troop here, what will it/its allies do". The gameplay is fun, and I want to recommend it, but not when there is an element of random "troop stupidity" which can all at once cost you a run. (@devs please look into the minimax algorithm since it appears that currently the troops only take the "best-right-now" move)

2025年8月评测： 重玩了一下，确实比之前测试版本增加了很多内容，可玩性大大提高了，值得一个好评。 运行略有不流畅，可以优化一下。 以下内容为2024年3月历史评测： 三章，每章3关，通一次需要过9关。 很单调的肉鸽游戏。目前只有三章，小怪和Boss种类特别少，自己能用的技能/卡牌也特别少。就肉鸽来说缺点很致命。 扮演神明也只是个噱头，没啥特色的系统，都是普通的肉鸽系统改个名字。不像天神，像中国神，每天努力挣扎求生存。 8小时，来回通了几遍就摸清楚了，没得玩了。

[h1]这个神不会翻手云覆手雨，也不会搬山填海[/h1] 《Godless》（《无神之世》）是由Danil Kalyupa自研自发的一款Roguelike回合制策略自走棋游戏，游戏里玩家饰演人类渎神弑神斗争之下的最后一位神明，但也已经岌岌可危了，施展神迹、召唤信徒来守卫自己最后的圣坛吧！ 游戏采用了六边形棋盘组成的战斗地图，弑神的人类大军除了第一波的先锋军一开始就在地图上外，其余的会按波次到达地图随机位置，地图上各地块都都有着不同的回合属性增长效果，只要双方兵力站立在上面就会每回合自动增长对应属性提高战力。 战斗的时候双方会根据位置按回合自动行进，相遇就会自动攻击，我方目的是消灭敌人多波次的有生力量，敌军则会不惜代价的摧毁我方圣坛。作为神明，我们在安置好圣坛位置后，就可以根据资源点每回合召唤信徒、施展法术或者改变地形属性来辅助信徒战斗，由于每轮游戏可召唤的信徒类别有限，因此信徒的搭配组合构筑就成了我们游戏能否顺利的关键点。信徒与地形、建筑的效果交互也是尤为重要，一些看似垃圾的信徒在特定的环境下会变得特别牛逼（比如熊搭配森林），这也是游戏需要思考的关键策略点。 整体而言，游戏也算是个相当不错的空闲代餐，用简单的地图加上简单的机制构筑出这么一个不简单的回合制策略自走棋，算是一个相当不错的沧海遗珠吧！ [quote]欢迎关注我们的鉴赏家:[url= https://store.steampowered.com/curator/35402982/]走心评测[/url] ←遵从内心，写出真实感受 欢迎加入我们Steam组:[url= https://steamcommunity.com/groups/ZXPC]走心评测[/url]←点击加入，一起探索游戏的乐趣 喜欢这篇评论，也麻烦点个赞，让更多人能够看到！[/quote]

[h1]带点肉鸽元素的回合策略自走棋[/h1] 《Godless》是一款Danil Kalyupa开发并发行的回合制策略Roguelike游戏。这款游戏融合了多种游戏元素，以回合制自走棋为核心机制，肉鸽元素的地图路线和相关内容为辅助，融合打造出了这样一款略显简陋却又趣味横生的游戏。 在游戏的游玩方面，本作的核心，是一个有一定策略性的回合制自走棋，玩家需要在一片由六边形区块组成的大陆上，选定一个安全的区域，放置自己的圣坛，并根据需求，选择具有不同效果的建筑或者英雄单位放置入场，而这些操作，都需要消耗魔力，魔力值只能每回合恢复1点。 回合开始后，这些英雄单位和敌方英雄单位就会开始移动，并进行攻击。这部分内容的运行逻辑，就是自走棋的模式，玩家无法对其进行操控，能做的只有释放一些法术进行辅助，或者等待魔力恢复后，向地图内增添新的英雄单位或建筑。 保护己方圣坛不被摧毁，并消灭所有波次的敌方单位，就是游戏战斗的目标。 体验上还是比较有趣的。根据玩家阵容和操作的区别，完全会导致出现不同的战局走向。 而在战斗部分之外，就是整体的强度运营了，当玩家结束战斗后，可以进行技能点数的分配，还有肉鸽元素中常见的地图线路机制，能够进入商店等区域，构筑完善自己的英雄组合以及法术。但由于游戏目前整体的内容还是较少的，这方面内容的还起不到太大的影响作用，并没有数量很多的构筑搭配可选。 总的来说，《Godless》属于一款能够去简单游玩一下的游戏，趣味性是有的。不过，游戏还是处于早期阶段，内容并不是特别的多，但游戏开发组本身的制作态度还是有的。目前，第四章节以及许多游戏性内容都落实完成，游戏内容的可玩性又有了一定程度的增长。可以期待一下其后续的不断发展。 [quote]关注[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/36224058/]老实人鉴赏家 [/url] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/laoshirenLSR]老实人评测[/url]：独立游戏爱好者聚集地，黄油绅士交流中心。 不错过游戏的亮点，不放过游戏的槽点，带给玩家最直观的测评感受。[/quote]

[h1]向日葵游戏评分【8/10】[/h1] 《Godless无神之世》是一款回合制Rogue策略游戏，在棋盘上保护圣坛，战胜对手。因为棋子是自动战斗，所以利用地形与法术排兵布阵尤为重要。而要说本作最吸引人的地方，则是灵活的构筑方向，游戏中的各种资源货币甚至可以互相转换，避免了纯靠运气完全看脸的尴尬局面。 [h1]欢迎大家关注我们的鉴赏家：https://store.steampowered.com/curator/28763059[/h1] [h1]和你一起寻找好玩的游戏，快来关注我们吧~微信公众号“向日葵游戏”、官方微博“向日葵游戏评测”[/h1]

一款自走棋卡组构筑肉鸽游戏，偏rex战旗。虽然没有特别亮眼之处，但好在玩法的多样且详实。局内根据功能分为法术/单位/地块，根据使用场合分为技能栏位/卷轴栏位；升级树方面包括技能栏位/独特被动能力/天赋三个模块，每个模块至少有三种升级方向。局外升级比较简单，多以成就系统式的导向指引玩家多次游戏，有点肝度。交互方向主要为单位与地块、地块与地块之间的两两效果交互，并没有一个主导的流派或者主题，因此这款游戏的前期开荒将非常痛苦——经常会感觉到交互之上还有交互。 游戏深度是有的，而且很多机制都和同类游戏相同，因此学习成本算不上高。但复杂确实也是复杂的，且在没有一个比较完整的机制渐进引导的前提下，对大量文本的阅读和交互效果的假想颇费时间。 p.s. 选择“遗产”环节以及对章节和大陆的描述里，好像还有进一步挖掘的空间，似乎能够拼凑出进一步的叙事框架。但暂时没有精力统筹了。 减面数多边形卡通风格，魔幻主题，2.5D俯视角场景。整体美术风格非常统一。频繁使用明暗对比和特效强调对象。ui方面总感觉缩放战场的操作有些别扭，结合其他按钮布置，总感觉很多都是贴合移动端的设计。 比较影响体验的是，游戏基本战斗方式是自走棋式，单位之间的索引均是自动的，但同时游戏又非常重视地块的功能——在玩家对单位移动的把控有限的情况下，很容易发生单位的行动超出玩家预期的情况。比如吹风地块效果会迫使单位退至指定方向，而如果一旦在狭小区域随机生成该地块，再加上糟糕的索敌机制，单位会因为向敌人方向移动而陷入走一步退一步的局面。游戏又比较缺乏低成本的位移效果，因此在移动机制上的减量很容易导致很多意外发生。或许应该引入一个对糟糕情况的保底机制，稳住一些游戏体验。 游戏素质还是比较强的，可玩性也很高。可以一试。 [h1] [quote] [table] [tr] [th] 🐱😸[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45217105][b] 不羁猫探索队 [/b][/url] | [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44339075][b] 不羁猫外文站 [/b][/url]😸🐱 [/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] 🧶🧶致力小型独游双语推广，主评叙事/策略类游戏🧶🧶 [/th] [/tr] [tr] [tr] [th] 欢迎开发者和小伙伴们一起交流 无限进步ฅ●ω●ฅ [/th] [/tr] [tr] [th] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/untamecat][b] 联系我们[/b][/url] |[url=https://indienova.com/author/mGvZ4JrvB86518/][b] 相关文章[/b][/url] [/th] [/tr]

Godless, developed and published by Danil Kalyupa, is an indie roguelike strategy game that flips a familiar narrative on its head. Instead of casting players as heroic champions or defenders of humanity, the game invites them to assume the role of the last surviving god—an ancient being bent on vengeance after the mortal world eradicated divine beings. This reversal is more than a narrative gimmick; it shapes the entire design philosophy, giving players control not over individual units or armies, but over the very forces of nature and power that embody a god’s wrath. In this sense, Godless offers a refreshingly original take on turn-based tactics, combining terrain manipulation, indirect unit influence, and roguelike progression into a unique and consistently engaging experience. Each run in Godless is structured around a series of procedurally generated continents, each inhabited by mortal heroes and their armies. The objective is simple in theory—defend your divine shrine and obliterate any resistance—but achieving that goal requires careful planning and adaptation. Unlike traditional strategy games where you micromanage each unit, Godless requires you to shape the battlefield itself, casting spells, modifying terrain, and deploying divine artifacts to turn the tide of battle. Your units, summoned through your godly powers, act on their own according to AI behaviors. This puts the emphasis on anticipation and influence, rather than direct control, which effectively reinforces the feeling that you’re a deity intervening from above rather than a general issuing orders. The tactical layer of the game shines through in its complex interactions between abilities, terrain, and enemy behavior. Shrines—each representing different styles of divine power—serve as your lifeline, and choosing the right combination of shrine powers and artifacts is key to survival. Some shrines reward aggression, others emphasize defense, resource control, or manipulation of the environment. Artifacts further diversify your playstyle, offering powerful passive or active abilities that can dramatically shift the way each run unfolds. These systems are tightly interwoven, making for a game where success depends not just on what tools you pick, but on how effectively you combine them to counter the evolving challenges of each new continent. Replayability is a central pillar of Godless, and it’s well-supported by the game’s procedural generation. Each continent features different terrain layouts, enemy hero compositions, and environmental hazards. Biomes evolve as you progress, introducing new mechanics and modifiers that require fresh strategies. Between combat encounters, you’ll make strategic decisions that influence the course of your campaign—selecting bonuses, choosing between risk-and-reward scenarios, or unlocking permanent upgrades. Even in defeat, progress carries forward in the form of new artifact unlocks or improved shrine capabilities, giving the game a satisfying sense of long-term growth. Visually, Godless favors clarity and readability over intricate detail. The battlefield is displayed on a clean hex grid, with stylized but simple graphics that keep your focus on positioning and tactics. While it lacks the visual flash of larger-budget titles, its minimalist aesthetic fits the abstract, godly perspective well. Animations are functional, if occasionally stiff, and the UI is generally well-designed, making it easy to track abilities, cooldowns, and unit behaviors. The audio design, while not particularly striking, adds to the atmosphere with a mix of ambient tones and understated sound effects that support the theme without overwhelming it. That said, the game does come with some limitations. The lack of direct unit control may be a turnoff for players used to more granular tactical gameplay, especially when your summoned creatures behave in ways that feel inefficient or unintuitive. Some players may also find the randomness of terrain generation or artifact availability to be punishing at times, particularly when a poorly synergized loadout makes a run feel unwinnable. The learning curve can be steep for those new to the genre or unfamiliar with roguelike mechanics, and the game doesn’t always explain its systems as clearly as it could. Despite these rough edges, Godless succeeds where it matters most. It delivers a consistently engaging loop of decision-making, experimentation, and adaptation. There’s a real thrill in discovering new artifact combinations, exploiting the environment to set clever traps, or turning a seemingly doomed battle into a divine slaughter through precise use of your shrine powers. Its thematic commitment to the “fallen god” perspective is more than skin deep—it shapes the gameplay in meaningful ways and gives the game a distinctive identity in a crowded genre. For its modest price, Godless offers tremendous value, especially for fans of tactical roguelikes and innovative strategy games. While it may not have the polish or visual fidelity of big-budget counterparts, it more than compensates with depth, originality, and replay potential. It's a thoughtful, cleverly designed title that challenges players to think differently about control, power, and persistence. Anyone looking for a strategy game that offers a fresh perspective—both narratively and mechanically—will likely find Godless to be a dark, compelling gem worth investing in. Rating: 9/10

After playing 20 hours in 2 days, I feel compelled to write a review. This game is excellent!! Don't hesitate to pick it up if you like tactical roguelites. The rest of the review is long and boring, and mostly praise to the dev as well as a little feedback. [h3]The good[/h3] This game could be a study example of good game design. There are many different systems at work, and they blend together well. Game is complex, but not complicated. Easy to pick up and learn, but requires thoughtful play on higher difficulties. Most "skills" (your active abilities) have a use, but some are inevitably better than others. The different status effects and modifiers are well thought out and probably the game's biggest strength: simple and (mostly) easy to understand, yet with plenty of options on how to interact with and benefit from them. There's no bloat. Why would any game ever need more than one type of DoT? Units act on their own, but you still have some agency through freezing or pushing them, or altering the terrain. Strikes a pretty good balance as a "semi-auto-battler". There are no card draws or dice rolls in battle. RNG only affects terrain generation, talent choices and shop stock. Rerolling shops and terrain is cheap, and the cost is static. The most powerful upgrade, the "gems", are the same every game and always accessible if you spend the resources. I think this is a good choice, and means you can start planning your strategy early. Losing runs to bad RNG is not a thing. There is a decent amount of content, but most of the replayability stems from trying different strategies at ever increasing difficulties. After 20 hours, there is still a lot yet to learn. Meta-progression is fairly fast, and once you have a few key upgrades, strategy is all that's holding you back. [h3]The "bad"[/h3] I wish there were a few more ways enemies could threaten you. All they can do is run at you and hit you in melee (except for one boss that attacks from range). Filling every hex with units and winning through attrition is a pretty good strategy. Graphics serviceable, nothing more. UI could definitely be improved upon. Performance is good, just some delay in menu transitions and when rerolling shops/terrain. I've noticed only 1 bug, related to exchanging currencies. It is annoying but does not affect gameplay. [h3]Summary[/h3] Excellent tactical roguelite apparently made by a single dev. Impressive execution for a one man endeavor, both in terms of gameplay balance and technical polish. Definitely underrated, but probably too complex for wide appeal. Yet, with better graphics, UI, and a fair bit of luck it could probably have gained considerably more traction. Will keep a close eye on their future projects.

Godless is a roguelite... autobattler? I like it a lot. It's actually sad to see such a game. Usually when I see a great game that didn't become a hit I can find some explanation, usually it's something with production values. But here the developer did everything right and just wasn't lucky. The game looks and sounds decent, the UI is completely adequate and makes it easy to play such a complex game. I see some people don't like randomness and indirect control, but I think they're missing the point, and it's hard to think of real complaints. Anyway, in this game you have your standard roguelite randomized path with various upgrades and resources, and you get into battles on hex grid. It's autobattler, as in you do not control any units, and instead just cast spells like summons and teraforming. You influence the battlefield so that your units win. Naturally there's a lot of complexity and all kinds of effects triggering other effects. Like you can summon a turtle unit, and every time it moves into a tile adjacent to water it moves again, so you can make "highays" for them to travel and also add some enchantment that triggers on unit move, or put beneficial buildings on those tiles, which can trigger something else as well. The variety is overwhelming and it's a joy to find new ways to make numbers big. There's metaprogression as well as very detailed difficulty setting, making every run feel very different from others. Maybe even too different - if I have any complaint it's that sometimes I feel like my success is mostly defined by the luck of the draw, and my own strategizing is secondary. I highly recommend this nice little gem.
